In [[probability theory]] and [[ergodic theory]], a '''Markov operator''' is an [[operator (mathematics)|operator]] on a certain [[function space]] that conserves the mass (the so-called [[Markov property]]). If the underlying [[measurable space]] is [[topological space|topologically]] sufficiently rich enough, then the Markov operator admits a [[probability kernel|kernel]] representation. Markov operators can be [[linear operator|linear]] or non-linear. Closely related to Markov operators is the '''Markov semigroup'''.<ref name="BGL">{{cite book|title=Analysis and Geometry of Markov Diffusion Operators|first1=Dominique|last1=Bakry|first2=Ivan|last2=Gentil|first3=Michel|last3=Ledoux|publisher=Springer Cham|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-00227-9}}</ref>

The definition of Markov operators is not entirely consistent in the literature. Markov operators are named after the Russian mathematician [[Andrey Markov]]. 
== Definitions ==
=== Markov operator ===
Let <math>(E,\mathcal{F})</math> be a [[measurable space]] and <math>V</math> a set of real, measurable functions <math>f:(E,\mathcal{F})\to (\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}))</math>.

A linear operator <math>P</math> on <math>V</math> is a '''Markov operator''' if the following is true<ref name="BGL" />{{rp|9-12}}
# <math>P</math> maps bounded, [[measurable function]] on bounded, measurable functions.
# Let <math>\mathbf{1}</math> be the constant function <math>x\mapsto 1</math>, then <math>P(\mathbf{1})=\mathbf{1}</math> holds. (''conservation of mass'' / ''Markov property'')
# If <math>f\geq 0</math> then <math>Pf\geq 0</math>. (''conservation of positivity'')

==== Alternative definitions ====
Some authors define the operators on the [[Lp space|L<sup>p</sup> spaces]] as <math>P:L^p(X)\to L^p(Y)</math> and replace the first condition (bounded, measurable functions on such) with the property<ref>{{cite book|first1=Tanja|last1=Eisner|first2=Bálint|last2=Farkas|first3=Markus|last3=Haase|first4=Rainer|last4=Nagel|date=2015|title=Operator Theoretic Aspects of Ergodic Theory|chapter=Markov Operators|series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics|volume=2727|publisher=Springer|place=Cham|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-16898-2|pages=249}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|first=Fengyu|last=Wang|title=Functional Inequalities Markov Semigroups and Spectral Theory|place=Ukraine|publisher=Elsevier Science|date=2006|page=3}}</ref>
:<math>\|Pf\|_Y = \|f\|_X,\quad \forall f\in L^p(X)</math>

=== Markov semigroup ===
Let <math>\mathcal{P}=\{P_t\}_{t\geq 0}</math> be a family of Markov operators defined on the set of bounded, measurables function on <math>(E,\mathcal{F})</math>. Then <math>\mathcal{P}</math> is a '''Markov semigroup''' when the following is true<ref name="BGL" />{{rp|12}}
# <math>P_0=\operatorname{Id}</math>.
# <math>P_{t+s}=P_t\circ P_s</math> for all <math>t,s\geq 0</math>.
# There exist a [[σ-finite measure]] <math>\mu</math> on <math>(E,\mathcal{F})</math> that is [[invariant measure|invariant]] under <math>\mathcal{P}</math>, that means for all bounded, positive and measurable functions <math>f:E\to \mathbb{R}</math> and every <math>t\geq 0 </math> the following holds
:::<math>\int_E P_tf\mathrm{d}\mu =\int_E f\mathrm{d}\mu</math>.

=== Dual semigroup ===
Each Markov [[semigroup]] <math>\mathcal{P}=\{P_t\}_{t\geq 0}</math> induces a ''dual semigroup'' <math>(P^*_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> through
:<math>\int_EP_tf\mathrm{d\mu} =\int_E f\mathrm{d}\left(P^*_t\mu\right).</math>
If <math>\mu</math> is invariant under <math>\mathcal{P}</math> then <math>P^*_t\mu=\mu</math>.

=== Infinitesimal generator of the semigroup ===
Let <math>\{P_t\}_{t\geq 0}</math> be a family of bounded, linear Markov operators on the [[Hilbert space]] <math>L^2(\mu)</math>, where <math>\mu</math> is an invariant measure. The '''infinitesimal generator''' <math>L</math> of the Markov semigroup <math>\mathcal{P}=\{P_t\}_{t\geq 0}</math> is defined as
:<math>Lf=\lim\limits_{t\downarrow 0}\frac{P_t f-f}{t},</math>
and the domain <math>D(L)</math> is the <math>L^2(\mu)</math>-space of all such functions where this limit exists and is in <math>L^2(\mu)</math> again.<ref name="BGL" />{{rp|18}}<ref>{{cite book|first=Fengyu|last=Wang|title=Functional Inequalities Markov Semigroups and Spectral Theory|place=Ukraine|publisher=Elsevier Science|date=2006|page=1}}</ref>
:<math>D(L)=\left\{f\in L^2(\mu): \lim\limits_{t\downarrow 0}\frac{P_t f-f}{t}\text{ exists and is in } L^2(\mu)\right\}.</math>

The [[carré du champ operator]] <math>\Gamma</math> measures how far <math>L</math> is from being a [[Derivation (differential algebra)|derivation]].

=== Kernel representation of a Markov operator ===
A Markov operator <math>P_t</math> has a kernel representation
:<math>(P_tf)(x)=\int_E f(y)p_t(x,\mathrm{d}y),\quad x\in E,</math>
with respect to some [[probability kernel]] <math>p_t(x,A)</math>, if the underlying measurable space <math>(E,\mathcal{F})</math> has the following sufficient topological properties:
# Each [[probability measure]] <math>\mu:\mathcal{F}\times \mathcal{F}\to [0,1]</math> can be decomposed as <math>\mu(\mathrm{d}x,\mathrm{d}y)=k(x,\mathrm{d}y)\mu_1(\mathrm{d}x)</math>, where <math>\mu_1</math> is the projection onto the first component and <math>k(x,\mathrm{d}y)</math> is a probability kernel.
# There exist a countable family that generates the [[σ-algebra]] <math>\mathcal{F}</math>.
If one defines now a [[σ-finite]] measure on <math>(E,\mathcal{F})</math> then it is possible to prove that every Markov operator <math>P</math> admits such a kernel representation with respect to <math>k(x,\mathrm{d}y)</math>.<ref name="BGL" />{{rp|7-13}}
